doc.title: Lou Donaldson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Blues in Badin and the hard lives of the plant workers
summary: Weekend blues came with drinking and fights among workers breathing aluminum fumes.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: Just stepping back again, was there any blues in town as a kid?
In my town? Yeah, people would sing blues.
Were you checking that out as a kid, or were you sheltered from it?

Not really. Not really, because they’d be drunk when they started doing it, and I’d get away from there quick, because I’d know eventually what was going to happen. There would be some fracases. So I’d get away. Because they lived a tough life. They was working in this Alcoa Aluminum factory at 222 degrees Fahrenheit, and on the weekend everybody was drunk. And now that I’m old and I look back, I can see exactly why. That was tough work. Tough work. Because you worked ten years breathing those fumes and things, you had to be well messed up.
You described the extraction process yesterday.
And there was no EPA at that time.
